Permutation inference for a policy's adoption

Source: R/policy_evaluation.R
perminf.Rd

Re-assigns the adoption dates across clusters (all the distinct assignments when there are few, random ones otherwise), re-estimates the difference in differences each time, and gives the share of assignments with an effect at least as large; for several outcomes, also the Westfall-Young stepdown p-values that hold the family-wise error rate.

Usage

perminf(
  data,
  unit,
  time,
  y,
  ftreat,
  cl = NULL,
  stat = c("t", "estimate"),
  reps = 999L,
  seed = NULL,
  ties = c("count", "strict")
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per unit and period.

unit, time

Column names: the unit and the period (numeric).

y

One outcome column, or several.

ftreat

Column name of the period a unit is first treated (NA, 0 or Inf for a unit never treated). Treatment is taken as staying on.

cl

Column name of the clusters (default the unit), or two column names for two-way clustering (Cameron, Gelbach and Miller 2011): \(V_a + V_b - V_{ab}\), each term with the small-sample factor of the dimension with fewer clusters, and t on its \(G - 1\) degrees of freedom. A composite cluster (district by month, say) is one column made with interaction().

stat

"t" (default) or "estimate".

reps

The number of random assignments (default 999).

seed

Optional seed.

ties

"count" (default): an assignment whose statistic equals the observed one counts (the observed assignment is among those enumerated, so the exact p-value is at least \(1/N\)); "strict": only larger ones count.

Value

A data frame of class rmbl_permutation, one row per outcome: outcome, estimate, statistic, p_value, pstpdn, assignments, exact; attribute null (the matrix of permuted statistics).

Details

The adoption period of each cluster (for example a judicial district's stage of a reform) is shuffled among the clusters, keeping the number of clusters adopting at each date, and plndid's estimate (statistic = "estimate") or t statistic ("t", the default) is recomputed. With \(b\) of \(R\) random assignments at least as extreme as observed, \(p = (b + 1)/(R + 1)\); when every distinct assignment is enumerated (their number is at most reps), \(p\) is the exact share. The test is Fisher's: it is valid in any sample when adoption dates were assigned at random across clusters.

For several outcomes, the same assignments give stpdnpv.

A placebo date is the same analysis with ftreat moved earlier, on the periods before the real adoption.

References

Fisher RA (1935). The Design of Experiments. Oliver and Boyd, Edinburgh.

Applied with the four stages of a reform permuted across districts: Acosta, Mejia and Zorro Medina (2023), see plndid.

See also

stpdnpv.

Examples

p <- polex()
perminf(p, "district", "month", c("crmrate", "arrrate"),
                      "refmonth",
                      cl = "region", reps = 199, seed = 3)
#>   outcome   estimate  statistic    p_value     pstpdn assignments exact
#> 1 crmrate -3.2316395 -19.516735 0.04166667 0.04166667          24  TRUE
#> 2 arrrate -0.2136969  -3.638159 0.12500000 0.12500000          24  TRUE
